This includes a network of national parks, biological reserves, wildlife refuges, and protected forests, covering rainforests, cloud forests, volcanoes, and coastlines. plain: The four card suits are widely believed to represent the four classes of medieval European society, based on their origins in French playing cards from the 15th century. Hearts represent the clergy, symbolizing the church. Spades, derived from the French word 'pique' (a pike or spearhead), represent the military or nobility. Diamonds, from the French 'carreau' (a tile), represent the merchant or wealthy trading class. Clubs, from the French 'trèfle' (a clover), represent the peasantry or agricultural workers. This interpretation isn't universally agreed upon, since different countries adapted suit symbols differently (Italian and Spanish decks originally used swords, cups, coins, and clubs), but the class-based explanation is the most common one taught today.

plain: Haft-sin is a ceremonial table arrangement set up for Nowruz, the Persian New Year, consisting of seven items whose names traditionally begin with the Persian letter 'sin' (S). Common items include: sabzeh (sprouted wheat or lentil grass, symbolizing rebirth), samanu (a sweet wheat pudding, symbolizing wealth and fertility), senjed (dried oleaster fruit, symbolizing love), seer (garlic, symbolizing health and medicine), seeb (apples, symbolizing beauty and health), somaq (sumac, symbolizing sunrise and the victory of good over evil), and serkeh (vinegar, symbolizing patience and wisdom that comes with age). Families often add other symbolic items too, like a mirror, candles, painted eggs, a goldfish, and a holy book or poetry collection, though the seven 'sin' items are the core requirement.

In the U.S. and Canada, green circles mean easy/beginner terrain with gentle slopes; blue squares mean intermediate, with moderate steepness; black diamonds mean advanced/expert terrain, often steep with obstacles; and double black diamonds mean expert-only, extremely steep or hazardous terrain. In Europe, a similar system uses green (easiest), blue (easy), red (intermediate/difficult), and black (expert), which can confuse American skiers since 'blue' means something different across the Atlantic. Always check the specific resort's trail map key before assuming, since exact difficulty within a color category can still vary a lot between resorts.

plain: Mozzarella and cheddar differ significantly in texture, flavor, and production. Mozzarella is a soft, fresh cheese traditionally made from buffalo or cow's milk using a stretching technique (pasta filata), giving it a stringy, elastic texture when melted and a mild, milky flavor. It's typically eaten fresh or melted, common on pizza and in caprese salads. Cheddar is a hard, aged cheese made through a different process involving cutting and stacking the curd ('cheddaring'), and it develops a much sharper, more complex flavor as it ages, ranging from mild to extra sharp depending on aging time (a few months to several years). Cheddar doesn't melt into strings the way mozzarella does; instead it melts into a smooth, creamy consistency.

plain: Andy Warhol's 'Oxidation Paintings,' informally called the 'piss paintings,' were created in 1977-78 by having people (including Warhol himself and studio assistants) urinate onto canvases coated with copper-based metallic paint. The uric acid in urine reacted chemically with the copper pigment, causing oxidation that produced unpredictable, painterly patterns of green, blue, and brown tones as it dried, similar to how metal rusts or patinas over time. Warhol was drawn to the randomness and lack of direct artistic 'hand' in the process, fitting his broader interest in mechanical or chance-based methods of image-making, and the works are often read as both a joke on abstract expressionist bravado (mimicking Jackson Pollock's action painting) and a genuine exploration of chemical process as art.

plain: Tail washout at the end of a turn usually happens because your weight shifts too far back or you lose pressure on the tail of the ski as the turn completes. If you're leaning back on your heels rather than staying centered, the tail can't grip the snow properly and skids out instead of carving cleanly. It can also happen if you're not finishing the turn with enough edge angle, or if you rush the transition into the next turn before fully completing the current one. To fix it, focus on maintaining forward pressure through your shins into your boots throughout the whole turn, especially at the finish, and consciously complete each turn before starting the next one rather than rushing the rhythm.

plain: Trekking is multi-day hiking, typically through remote or mountainous terrain, often involving overnight stays in tents, huts, or local villages along the route. Several distinct types exist. Alpine trekking crosses high mountain terrain, sometimes involving snow, ice, or technical passes, requiring more specialized gear. Desert trekking takes place in arid regions, requiring careful water and heat management. Jungle or rainforest trekking involves dense, humid terrain with different navigation and wildlife-awareness challenges. Cultural or village trekking focuses on passing through and staying in local communities, emphasizing cultural exchange alongside the physical activity. Each type demands different preparation, from fitness level to specialized equipment and altitude acclimatization.
